findings.title: Kernel vulnerability is unmitigated: spectre_v2
findings.description: The kernel exposes hardware vulnerability mitigation status (Spectre, Meltdown, L1TF, MDS, etc.) through sysfs. NULQ records whether each mitigation is active, partial or absent.
findings.explanation: Kernel reports "vulnerable" status "Vulnerable: eIBRS with unprivileged eBPF" for hardware vulnerability spectre_v2. Value: Vulnerable: eIBRS with unprivileged eBPF.
findings.impact: An unmitigated or partially mitigated hardware vulnerability may be exploitable by local processes to leak memory or bypass isolation boundaries.
findings.remediation: Update the kernel and firmware, enable mitigations via boot parameters, and consult the distribution's hardening guidance for each vulnerability.
limitations: Mitigation status is read from sysfs; NULQ does not test whether an exploit applies to the running kernel.
Some mitigations carry performance costs and may be intentionally disabled.

findings.title: Kernel hardening parameter is below the recommended baseline
findings.description: A security-relevant kernel parameter is set below a conservative baseline, expanding the attack surface available to unprivileged users.
findings.explanation: The kernel parameter kernel.kptr_restrict is 0, which does not meet the baseline (at least 1). Kernel pointers are exposed through several interfaces; unrestricted values aid exploit development.
findings.impact: The weaker setting expands what unprivileged local processes can observe or exercise in the kernel. It is a hardening gap, not by itself a vulnerability.
limitations: Baselines are conservative defaults; some environments require different values for workload compatibility.
This rule does not assess whether a known exploit applies to the running kernel.

findings.title: Kernel hardening parameter is below the recommended baseline
findings.description: A security-relevant kernel parameter is set below a conservative baseline, expanding the attack surface available to unprivileged users.
findings.explanation: The kernel parameter kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is 0, which does not meet the baseline (at least 1). Unprivileged BPF program loading has been a recurring source of kernel privilege-escalation primitives.
findings.impact: The weaker setting expands what unprivileged local processes can observe or exercise in the kernel. It is a hardening gap, not by itself a vulnerability.
findings.remediation: Set kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1 in /etc/sysctl.d/ or at boot.
limitations: Baselines are conservative defaults; some environments require different values for workload compatibility.
This rule does not assess whether a known exploit applies to the running kernel.

findings.title: Kernel hardening parameter is below the recommended baseline
findings.description: A security-relevant kernel parameter is set below a conservative baseline, expanding the attack surface available to unprivileged users.
findings.explanation: The kernel parameter kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone is 1, which does not meet the baseline (0). Unprivileged user namespaces widen the kernel surface reachable by unprivileged users on distributions that expose this switch.
findings.impact: The weaker setting expands what unprivileged local processes can observe or exercise in the kernel. It is a hardening gap, not by itself a vulnerability.
findings.remediation: Set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 where the workload does not require unprivileged namespaces.
limitations: Baselines are conservative defaults; some environments require different values for workload compatibility.
This rule does not assess whether a known exploit applies to the running kernel.

findings.title: Unprivileged user namespace clone is enabled
findings.description: The kernel allows unprivileged users to create user namespaces, widening the kernel attack surface reachable from unprivileged processes.
findings.explanation: kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone is 1, allowing unprivileged users to create user namespaces. This widens the kernel surface reachable by unprivileged local processes.
findings.impact: User namespaces have been a recurring source of kernel privilege-escalation primitives. Enabling them for unprivileged users increases exploitability of kernel bugs.
findings.remediation: Set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 in /etc/sysctl.d/ or at boot, unless a workload requires unprivileged namespaces.
limitations: This rule does not assess whether a known exploit applies to the running kernel.
Some containers and sandboxed workloads require unprivileged namespaces to function.

findings.title: Container marker file present
findings.description: Marker files and sockets indicate the assessment target is a container or has container runtime tooling installed. NULQ never connects to the Docker socket or contacts any runtime.
findings.explanation: /.dockerenv was observed on the assessed system. This indicates container runtime tooling or a containerised assessment target.
findings.impact: Container runtime presence expands the privilege surface: container escapes, socket mounting and runtime configuration are out of scope for this rule.
findings.remediation: If the Docker socket is present and accessible to unprivileged users, restrict its permissions. Ensure container runtimes are not exposed to untrusted workloads.
limitations: Indicator presence does not mean the runtime is running, accessible or exploitable.
NULQ never connects to any socket or contacts any runtime.

limitations: Permission checks use ownership and mode bits together with POSIX ACLs when ACL state is observed; security-module policy is not evaluated, and unreadable or malformed ACL state is reported as unknown rather than assumed.

Process observations cover numeric identity, lifecycle and executable-path context only; environments, command lines, memory maps and file descriptors are never read, so process intent and runtime behavior are not assessed.
